name: Hana Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Hana. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We farm 60 hectares of hill ground that's been in my husband Mehmet's family for three generations. There are 150 sheep, twenty dairy cows that we still milk in the old parlour, hay, and a field of potatoes. I do the milking morning and evening, the calves and the hens, and Mehmet does the sheep and the tractor work. His parents live in the old farmhouse and we live in the bungalow we built next to it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the whole family is on the land, and the children see their grandparents every day. What's hard is the milk cheque: the dairy pays us less than it costs to make, some months. We took a mortgage to build the bungalow and we have less than a month of money put by. I don't use computers if I can help it; our son Emre does the online forms for the subsidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, people should get back to real work and stop chasing gadgets. I'd say it after Friday prayers to the other farming families. I wouldn't put anything online; I don't go online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't help us at all. The dairy can still drop small farms like ours whenever it likes, and the milk price is the milk price. Our worry was never computers, it's the supermarket squeezing the dairy and the dairy squeezing us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep milking and keep the sheep, the same as always. I'd cut back on the shopping and make more at home, like my mother did. If money got very tight, Mehmet's brother has said he'd lend us something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, and a bit cross. The same old worries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways, which we only have once a month anyway. Then new clothes; Elif can wear Emre's old coats. I won't cut the children's school trips, that's where I draw the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Mehmet's brother. How do you feel about borrowing from family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's better than borrowing from the bank or asking the government. Family looks after family; that's how it's always been here. I'd still hate asking.

say: People should get back to **real work** and stop chasing gadgets.
I'd say it to **farming families** after Friday prayers, not online.
think: The plateau **doesn't help** us at all.
The dairy can still **drop small farms** like ours whenever it likes.
do: Keep **milking and the sheep** as always.
Cut the shopping and **make more at home**.
Borrow from **Mehmet's brother** if money gets very tight.
feel: **Tired** and **a bit cross** about the same old worries.
S0.quote: Our worry was never computers, it's the supermarket squeezing the dairy and the dairy squeezing us.
fieldNote: She blames the **supermarket and dairy** chain, not technology.
**Family loans** come before banks or government help.
Her line in the sand is the **children's school trips**.

steps.text: Keep milking the twenty cows twice a day
Cut takeaways and new clothes, and cook more from scratch
Borrow from Mehmet's brother if the milk cheque falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farming will be all right because you can't milk a cow with a computer. I'd say people should learn real trades, with apprenticeships, not sit at screens. I'd tell that to anyone at the school gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the paperwork that frightens me. The dairy will send orders and prices through some program, the government will want the subsidy forms done by computer, and I won't understand any of it. My hands are fine; it's the forms that could cost us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the farm the same and let Emre handle the computer side, even though he's only fourteen. I'd ask the young woman at the farmers' advice office in town to help us once a year. I'd wait and see before changing anything on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit ashamed. I don't want my fourteen-year-old son doing my farm paperwork for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Emre can't manage the forms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd pay someone, which we can't afford, or we'd miss the subsidy. Last year he nearly missed the deadline because of exams. I lay awake for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd learn yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe how to read the dairy's messages on the phone. Nothing more than that. I'm not too old, I'm just not interested.

say: You **can't milk a cow** with a computer.
People should learn **real trades** through apprenticeships, not sit at screens.
think: The **paperwork** frightens me more than anything on the farm.
My hands are fine, but the **subsidy forms** could cost us.
do: Ask the **farmers' advice office** for help once a year.
**Wait and see** before changing the farm.
feel: **Uneasy** and **a bit ashamed** that her son does her paperwork.
S1.quote: I don't want my fourteen-year-old son doing my farm paperwork for me.
fieldNote: For her, thinking AI shows up as **paperwork she can't handle**.
Leaning on a **14-year-old son** is a real weak spot.
She calls herself **not interested**, not too old.

steps.text: Have Emre file the subsidy forms online each spring
Book a yearly session at the farmers' advice office
Leave the farm unchanged until the dairy forces something

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when nobody puts the brakes on, and that families will have to stick together. I'd vote for whoever promised to protect family farms. I'd say it at the mosque and in the village shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, 2028 hardly touches my hands, but by 2031 the big dairies would have robot milkers and robot feeders, and twenty cows on a hill farm can't compete with that. The dairy would drop us. Sheep on steep ground might last longer, but sheep alone don't pay a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sell the dairy cows while they're still worth something, before every small farm tries to sell at once. We'd grow more potatoes and sell them at the farm gate. And the whole family would live in the farmhouse with Mehmet's parents so we could rent out the bungalow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Elif about the cows going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter the cows are going to another farm where they'll be looked after. Elif names every calf, so she'd cry. I'd probably cry with her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept government help in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was for everyone, like the farm subsidy, maybe. I don't want handouts. I'd rather work for it, but you can't work for what isn't there.

say: This is what happens when **nobody brakes**, so families must stick together.
I'd vote for whoever promises to **protect family farms**.
think: By 2031, **robot dairies** make twenty cows on a hill farm worthless.
Sheep on steep ground might last, but **sheep alone** don't pay a mortgage.
do: Sell the **dairy cows** before every small farm tries at once.
Move in with Mehmet's parents and **rent the bungalow**.
S2.quote: Sheep on steep ground might last longer, but sheep alone don't pay a mortgage.
fieldNote: She knows the **dairy is the first** part of the farm to go.
**Renting the bungalow** and sharing a house is her family-first answer.
She'd accept help only if it was **for everyone**, not a handout.

steps.text: Sell the twenty dairy cows in the first year
Grow more potatoes and sell them at the farm gate
Move into the farmhouse with Mehmet's parents and rent the bungalow
Vote for the party promising to protect family farms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for sensible people to get ready, without the government running everything. I'd say young people should take apprenticeships. I'd say it to the other mothers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the same ending, but the robots in 2034 give us time to sell the cows slowly and properly. Emre would be nineteen and could choose a trade. I'm worried, but it's not tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell a few cows each year rather than all at once. Someone has to fix the robots, so my son should be an apprentice at the machinery dealer. I'd keep the sheep and potatoes going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can sleep. There's time to do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Mehmet think about selling the cows?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mehmet's father bought the first cows, so it would hurt Mehmet. But he knows the numbers. He'd want to wait, and I'd have to push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use the technology yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Emre can learn it, that's his generation. I'll do what I know.

say: Five years is enough for **sensible people** to get ready.
Young people should take **apprenticeships** instead of waiting for government.
think: Robots in 2034 give time to **sell the cows slowly**.
**Emre** would be nineteen and could choose a trade.
do: Push Emre toward an **apprenticeship** at the machinery dealer.
S3.quote: Someone has to fix the robots, so my son should be an apprentice at the machinery dealer.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **plan an orderly exit** from dairy.
She puts **her son's trade** at the centre of the family's future.
She'll push her husband, whose **father's legacy** is in the herd.

steps.text: Sell four or five dairy cows each autumn
Arrange an apprenticeship for Emre at the machinery dealer
Keep the 150 sheep and the potato field going

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and farmers should be left to get on with it. I'd say families should prepare their children. Not much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots in 2039 means I'd be 56 and Emre and Elif grown. The milk price would still be a worry the whole time. But we could keep the farm as it is for most of my working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming as we are. I'd put a little by for Elif's studies and help Emre into a trade. I'd still refuse the computer, unless the dairy made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in the old way. The cows worry me more than robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your faith community do in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our community helps each other: weddings, funerals, bad harvests. If farms struggled, people would share. That matters more than any scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd regret not doing in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not learning a bit about the computers. I'd be stubborn about it. I'd probably regret that.

say: Ten years is plenty, and farmers should be **left to get on** with it.
Families should **prepare their children** for what's coming.
think: Robots in 2039 come when **the kids are grown**.
The **milk price** would still worry me the whole decade.
do: Keep **farming as we are** with the cows, sheep and potatoes.
Save a little each month for **Elif's studies**.
Help **Emre into a trade** when he leaves school.
feel: **Uneasy** in the old way; cows worry her more than robots.
S4.quote: The cows worry me more than robots do.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **keep the farm** for most of her working life.
Her safety net is **faith and community**, not government.
She admits she might **regret refusing** to learn computers.

steps.text: Keep milking and running the sheep as now
Put a little aside each month for Elif's studies
Help Emre find a trade apprenticeship at sixteen

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the cows would have to go in a hurry and so would half our income. What would help is a fair price for milk and a dairy that keeps buying from small farms. And apprenticeships for young people, so Emre has a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the grandparents. Mehmet's father still walks the hill every morning at eighty. A farm with robots and no family on it isn't a farm, it's a factory with grass.

headlineQuote: A farm with robots and no family on it isn't a farm, it's a factory with grass.
portrait: Hana, 43, farms her husband's family **hill farm** with 150 sheep and twenty dairy cows.
Mehmet's parents live next door; the family is **close and faith-centred**.
She never uses computers, and her son Emre **does the subsidy forms**.
She blames **the supermarket and dairy** for her money worries, not technology.
In fast worlds she'd **sell the cows** and lean on family rather than government.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the dairy cows and half the income would go in a hurry.
whatWouldHelp: A **fair milk price**, a dairy that keeps small farms, and **apprenticeships** for the young.
